extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers studying algebraic geometry; readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea'
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the textbook criteria and equivalent characterizations for flat morphisms, local/infinitesimal/slicing criteria for flatness, generic flatness/Grothendieck freeness, constancy results in flat families, and equivalent formulations of smooth and étale morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat of relative dimension n (Definition 24.5.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is a flat morphism that is locally of finite type, and all fibres of π have pure dimension n, we say that π is flat of relative dimension n. (When one says a morphism is flat of relative dimension n, the locally finite type hypotheses are implied.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 24.5.11 motivates the 'locally finite type' hypothesis: it ensures a reasonable class of morphisms and that the notion is preserved by base change. Use the definition when wanting a notion of 'flat family with fiber dimension n'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: pure dimension of total space vs flat of relative dimension (Exercise 24.5.I)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π : X → Y a flat morphism of finite type k-schemes with Y equidimensional, the following are equivalent: (i) X has pure dimension dim Y + n; (ii) π is flat of relative dimension n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to check relative dimension by comparing total-space dimension; useful practice exercise connecting geometry of X and relative flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity of relative dimension under composition (Exercise 24.5.J)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y and ρ : Y → Z are morphisms of locally Noetherian schemes, flat of relative dimensions m and n respectively (hence locally of finite type), then the composition ρ ∘ π is flat of relative dimension m+n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when checking relative dimensions in composed flat families; hint: use Exercise 24.5.I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of 'flat of relative dimension n' under base change (Exercise 24.5.K)
rubrics_metrics.description: The property of a morphism being 'flat of relative dimension n' is preserved by arbitrary base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check this, show fiber dimension is preserved (use Exercise 12.2.M). This is one reason for the locally finite type hypothesis in the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grothendieck's Generic Freeness Lemma (24.5.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose B is a Noetherian integral domain. Then every finitely generated B-algebra satisfies the following: for each finitely generated A-module M there exists a nonzero f ∈ B such that Mf is a free Bf-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved via a sequence of exercises in the text. This lemma is a key technical input to generic flatness results and should be used to reduce to free (hence flat) situations after inverting an element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic flatness (Exercise 24.5.R and Theorem 24.5.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is a finite type morphism to a Noetherian integral scheme and F a coherent sheaf on X, then there is a dense open subset U ⊂ Y over which F is flat. (Improved version 24.5.16: for π of finite type with Y reduced and F of finite type quasi-coherent, there is dense open U such that F|π^{-1}(U) is of finite presentation over π^{-1}(U) and flat over U.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special important case: F = O_X gives a dense open over which π is flat. Use Grothendieck Generic Freeness Lemma as the main input; the improved form requires finiteness/presentation hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness is an open condition (Theorem 24.5.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For π : X → Y a finite type morphism of locally Noetherian schemes and F a coherent sheaf on X, the locus of points of X at which F is Y-flat is open in X. (b) If π is closed (e.g., proper), then the locus in Y over which F is flat (i.e., points q ∈ Y for which F is flat at all p ∈ π^{-1}(q)) is open in Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) reduces to a commutative algebra statement (Mat2, Thm. 24.3 or EGA). Noetherian hypotheses can be weakened by replacing with local finite presentation hypotheses on π.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local criterion for flatness over a Noetherian local ring (Theorem 24.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (A,m) is a Noetherian local ring and M a finitely generated A-module. Then M is flat if and only if Tor^A_1(M, A/m) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miraculous: flatness over all of Spec A can be detected at the closed point. Caution: the finite generation hypothesis is necessary (example given in text). Use when working with finitely generated modules over local rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: More general local criterion for flatness (Theorem 24.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (A,m) → (B,n) is a local morphism of Noetherian local rings, and M is a finitely generated A-module. Then M is B-flat if and only if Tor^B_1(M, B/n) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Artin–Rees / Krull Intersection and reduction to checking injectivity of I ⊗_B M → M for ideals I of B. Helpful preliminary exercises (24.6.A–P) guide the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitesimal criterion for flatness (Exercise 24.6.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (A,m) → (B,n) is a local homomorphism of local rings and M a finitely generated A-module. If for each t ≥ 0, M/(n^t M) is flat over B/n^t, then M is flat over B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine with Exercise 24.6.A to recover the local criterion 24.6.2. The proof follows the proof of Theorem 24.6.2 and uses reduction mod n^t and exactness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slicing criterion for flatness (Theorem 24.6.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (B,n) → (A,m) is a local morphism of Noetherian local rings, M a finitely generated A-module, and t ∈ B a non-zerodivisor. Then M is B-flat if and only if (i) t is not a zerodivisor on M, and (ii) M/tM is flat over B/(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: slicing by an effective Cartier divisor on the target. The proof reduces to comparing Tor over B and B/(t) (Lemma 24.6.6). Useful to prove flatness by induction on dimension or to check behavior under divisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tor comparison lemma for slicing (Lemma 24.6.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If t ∈ B is not a zerodivisor on M, then for any B/(t)-module N and any i, Tor^B_i(M,N) = Tor^{B/(t)}_i(M/tM, N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by taking a free resolution of M and reducing mod t; used in the slicing criterion to translate Tor-vanishing between B and B/(t).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local slicing in the source and relative effective Cartier divisors (Exercise 24.6.F and Remark 24.6.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a B-algebra with A and B Noetherian and M a finitely generated A-module, and f ∈ B is such that multiplication by f is injective on M/nM for all primes n, then if M is B-flat, M/fM is also B-flat. More generally, under flat local homomorphism hypotheses and A essentially finitely presented, if f ∈ A is a non-zerodivisor in B/mB then A/f is flat over B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: a relative effective Cartier divisor on a flat morphism is flat over the base. Noetherian hypotheses can be removed under appropriate finite presentation assumptions (see Stacks tag 046Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibral Flatness Theorem (24.6.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a commuting diagram X --π→ Y and X --τ→ Z with ρ : Y → Z and points p ∈ X, q = π(p) ∈ Y, r = τ(p) ∈ Z and a finitely presented sheaf F on X (with either X,Y locally Noetherian or ρ,τ locally of finite presentation), the following are equivalent: (a) F is τ-flat at p and F|_r is π_r-flat at p; (b) ρ is flat at q and F is π-flat at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a criterion relating flatness of the base-change ρ and flatness of F as a family; useful to reduce flatness questions to fibers and base morphisms. The proof reduces to affine/Noetherian cases and uses commutative algebra results from EGA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness implies constant Euler characteristic in projective families (Theorem 24.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π : X → Y is a projective morphism of locally Noetherian schemes and F a coherent sheaf on X flat over Y. Then χ(X_q, F|_{X_q}) = Σ (-1)^i dim_{κ(q)} H^i(X_q, F|_{X_q}) is a locally constant function of q ∈ Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: reduce to affine target and twist so higher cohomology vanishes; the Čech complex terms are flat, so pushforward Γ(π_* F(m)) is locally free and hence has locally constant rank; tensoring with κ(q) computes the fiber cohomology. Noetherian hypotheses ensure coherence of π_* F(m). Use this as a necessary condition for flatness (converses given in exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert polynomial and other numerical invariants are locally constant in flat projective families (Corollary 24.7.2 & 24.7.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 24.7.1, the Hilbert polynomial of F|_{X_q} is locally constant in q. For a projective flat morphism X → Y with Y connected, the degree of the fiber, the fiber dimension, and the arithmetic genus are constant functions of q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Theorem 24.7.1 to twists and use definitions of degree and genus in terms of Euler characteristics / Hilbert polynomials. Useful for detecting pathologies and for constructing invariants of families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of line bundles is locally constant on flat projective families of curves (Corollary 24.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invertible sheaf L on a flat projective family of curves has locally constant degree on the fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: L is flat (locally isomorphic to O_X), so χ(X_q, L_q) is locally constant; degree is defined as χ(L_q) − χ(O_{X_q}). Use for comparing line bundles in families (e.g., defining Pic^0 and Néron–Severi discussions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired alternate definitions for smooth and étale morphisms (25.1.5 and Exercise 25.2.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed equivalent characterizations: π : X → Y is smooth of relative dimension n iff (i) π is locally of finite presentation, (ii) π is flat of relative dimension n, and (iii) Ω_{X/Y} is locally free of rank n. Similarly, π is étale iff π is locally of finite presentation, flat, and Ω_{X/Y} = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the 'desired' characterizations and are proved equivalent to the original definitions (Definition 13.6.2) in Theorem 25.2.2 and Exercise 25.2.B. They are the practical criteria often used in checking smoothness/étaleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterizations of smooth morphisms (Theorem 25.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism π : X → Y the following are equivalent: (i) π is smooth of relative dimension n (Definition 13.6.2); (ii) π is locally finitely presented and flat of relative dimension n, and Ω_π is locally free of rank n; (iii) π is locally finitely presented and flat, and the fibers are smooth k-schemes of pure dimension n; (iv) same as (iii) with geometric fibers smooth of pure dimension n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use any of these equivalent formulations depending on which hypotheses are easiest to verify. The theorem motivates checking flatness plus differential/ fiber conditions rather than only the original definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent formulations of étale morphisms (Exercise 25.2.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following are equivalent for π : X → Y: (a) π is étale; (b) π is smooth and unramified; (c) π is locally finitely presented, flat, and unramified; (d) π is locally finitely presented, flat, and for each q ∈ Y, π^{-1}(q) is a disjoint union of schemes Spec K where K is a finite separable extension of κ(q); (e) locally finitely presented, flat, and for each geometric point q of Y, π^{-1}(q) is the scheme-theoretic disjoint union of copies of q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These give practical fiberwise and algebraic characterizations of étaleness (e.g., finite separable residue field extensions on fibers). Exercise 25.2.C guides deriving these equivalences; choose the formulation best suited to the problem at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warnings and anti-patterns: necessity of finite generation/Noetherian hypotheses and behavior of unramified maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite generation hypotheses are often necessary (e.g., local criterion 24.6.1 fails without finite generation). The 'locally finite type/presentation' hypotheses are important to make classes of morphisms behave reasonably (e.g., preserved by base change). Unramified morphisms do not require flatness — examples show pathological behaviors (e.g., Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) → Spec k is unramified but not a fibration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check the presence/absence of Noetherian, finite type, finite presentation, or finite generation hypotheses before applying these criteria. Be cautious using criteria that drop flatness or finiteness conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Čech complexes and flatness to deduce locally free pushforwards (proof technique in Theorem 24.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: When higher cohomology vanishes after twisting, the Čech complex computing global sections consists of flat modules, so exactness plus flatness implies the front term (Γ(π_* F(m))) is flat and hence locally free; tensoring with residue fields then computes fiber Hilbert functions/Euler characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard technique: ensure sufficient twisting so higher cohomology vanishes (Serre vanishing) and then use flatness of terms to deduce base-change properties and local freeness of pushforwards. Useful in proving constancy results.
